## Learning Objectives

1. Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate
2. Describe how the size and bias of a sample affects the [sampling distribution]{.alert}
3. Calculate the [standard error of the mean]{.alert}
4. Calculate [confidence intervals]{.alert} using the [standard error of the mean]{.alert}
5. Know how to correctly interpret [confidence intervals]{.alert}
6. Display and correctly interpret [error bars]{.alert} on a graph

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

Back to our uhu example

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=3.25, cache=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
# NOTE: this figure needs the image /img/uhu4measure.png, which is not
# currently in the project. Restore that asset and set eval=TRUE to render.
uhu <- image_read("/img/uhu4measure.png") |>
    image_flop() |>
    image_resize(geometry = geometry_size_percent(50)) |>
    image_transparent("white")

uhuloa <- function(loa = 1) {
    par(mar = rep(0, 4))
    plot(0:50, type = "n", axes = FALSE)
    rect(-0.5, 6, 50.5, 13, col = "gray")
    text(0.5, 7, labels = "cm", cex = 0.75)

    segments(x0 = 0, y0 = 12, x1 = 50, lwd = 0.5)
    segments(x0 = 0:50, y0 = 10, y1 = 12, lwd = 0.5)
    segments(x0 = (0:49) + 0.5, y0 = 10.75, y1 = 12, lwd = 0.5)
    segments(x0 = seq(0.1, 49.9, by = 0.1), y0 = 11.25, y1 = 12, lwd = 0.25)

    text(0:50, rep(11, 51), labels = 0:50, cex = 0.5, pos = 1)

    xr <- par("usr")[1:2]
    p <- 1
    grid.raster(uhu, x = (0 - xr[1]) / diff(xr),
                hjust = 0, width = loa * 50 / diff(xr))
}

uhuloa(0.8)
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

5 sections produced 5 [samples]{.alert} from an unknown [population]{.alert}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
uhu <- read.csv("../data/section_sample_uhu.csv")
uhu <- uhu[uhu$length_cm > 18, ]
uhu$Section <- sprintf("%02d", uhu$Section)
uhu <- uhu[uhu$Section != "NA", ]

uhu_p <- ggplot(uhu, aes(x = Section, y = length_cm, color = Section)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    scale_color_viridis_d(alpha = 0.5)

uhu_p
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

We can calculate the [estimate]{.alert} of the means for each [samples]{.alert}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
uhu_pm <- uhu_p + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar",
                               width = 0.75, color = viridis::viridis(5))

uhu_pm
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

Look at the collection of all [estimates]{.alert} of the means

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
uhu_m <- group_by(uhu, Section) |>
    summarize(m = mean(length_cm)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(x = m, y = 0, color = Section)) +
    geom_point(shape = 18, size = 5) +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.line.y = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
          axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
    ylab("") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 3)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(28.5, 32))
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

Now imagine we could collect many **many** **MANY** samples and look at the collection of all their mean [estimates]{.alert}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=3, fig.height=3}
                                 y = 0, Section = "06"),
               mapping = aes(x = x, y = y),
               shape = 18, size = 5,
               color = "gray", alpha = 0.5)

uhu_s
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

The [estimated]{.alert} means of those many **many** **MANY** [samples]{.alert} come from the [sampling distribution]{.alert}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=3.5, fig.height=2.5}
uhu_s + stat_function(fun = \(x) 4 * dnorm(x, 30.25, sd = 0.75),
                      color = "black") +
    ylab("\"Probability\"") +
    theme(axis.line.y = element_line())
```

## Describe the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of an estimate

The [sampling distribution]{.alert} describes all the possible outcomes (and how likely or unlikely those outcomes are) of taking infinite hypothetical [samples]{.alert} from the same [population]{.alert} and calculating an [estimate]{.alert} (like the mean) for each.

## Describe how the size and bias of a sample affects the [sampling distribution]{.alert}

* Greater sample size ($N$) decreases variability in the [sampling distribution]{.alert}
* Biased samples shift the sampling distribution away from the true population parameter

## Greater sample size decreases variability among estimates

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
set.seed(123)
dfsamp <- lapply(c(20, 40, 80), function(n) {
    p <- replicate(1000, {
        s <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
        mean(s)
    })

    data.frame(p = p, n = n)
})

dfsamp <- do.call(rbind, dfsamp)

dfse <- group_by(dfsamp, n) |>
    summarize(x = mean(p) - 10 / sqrt(n[1]),
              xend = mean(p) + 10 / sqrt(n[1])) |>
    ungroup()

dfsamp$n <- paste("n =", dfsamp$n)
dfse$n <- paste("n =", dfse$n)
dfse$y <- dfse$yend <- 50

names(dfsamp)[2] <- names(dfse)[1] <- "Sample size"

sampdp <- ggplot(dfsamp, aes(p)) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(`Sample size`)) +
    geom_histogram(show.legend = FALSE, fill = "gray") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
          strip.text = element_text(size = 18)) +
    xlab("Mean length (cm)")

sampdp
```

## The [standard error]{.alert} quantifies the spread of estimates

> The [standard error]{.alert} of an estimate is the standard deivation of the estimate's sampling distribution

You can calculate a standard error for any population parameter, but we will start with the standard error of the sample mean

## Standard error of the sample mean

|  |  |
|---:|:---|
| Sample mean: | $\overline{Y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n Y_i$ |
| Sample variance: | $s^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^n (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2$ |
| Sample standard deviation: | $s = \sqrt{s^2}$ |
| Sample mean [standard error]{.alert}: | $\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ |

## Standard error of the sample mean

|  |  |
|---:|:---|
| Sample mean: | $\overline{Y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n Y_i$ |
| Sample mean [standard error]{.alert}: | $\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ |

The [standard error]{.alert} is an *estimate* of an **estimate** (e.g. the mean)

As with any estimate we don't know the true value, but it's our best guess

## Greater sample size decreases the [standard error]{.alert}!!!

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
sampdp +
    geom_segment(data = dfse,
                 aes(x = x, y = y, yend = yend, xend = xend),
                 color = "#DD8739", linewidth = 2) +
    ylab("Count")
```

## Key take-aways:

- [Standard error]{.alert} describes the spread of the [sampling distribution]{.alert}
- The [standard error]{.alert} is the standard deviation of the [sampling distribution]{.alert}
- The [standard error]{.alert} is **not** the standard deviation of the data (SE < SD *always*)
- Greater sample size decreases the [standard error]{.alert}!

## Calculating the [standard error]{.alert} in *R*

Read in the uhu data you all generated

```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
uhu <- read.csv("../data/section_sample_uhu.csv")
```

```{r echo = TRUE}
head(uhu, n = 3)
```

## Calculating the [standard error]{.alert} in *R*

Calculate estimate of standard deviation for Section 01

```{r echo = TRUE}
# subset data to just section 01
uhu_01 <- subset(uhu, Section == "01")

# calcualte SD
s <- sd(uhu_01$length_cm)
s
```

From `s` we can calculate [standard error]{.alert}

```{r echo = TRUE}
se <- s / sqrt(length(uhu_01))
se
```

## Review of [standard error]{.alert} and [sampling distribution]{.alert}

If we went out again and collected a different sample of 20 individuals (*many* **many** times) would we get roughly the same estimate or not? **SE tells us!**

## Review of [standard error]{.alert} and [sampling distribution]{.alert}

If we went out again and collected a different sample of 20 individuals (*many* **many** times) would we get roughly the same estimate or not? **SE tells us!**

- The wider the sampling distribution, the bigger the SE
- (The SE is the SD of the sampling distribution)
- The bigger the SE, the less likely we are to get similar estimates across repeated samples
- The less likely we are to get similar estimates across samples, the less [confident]{.alert} we are in the accuracy of any one sample

# Why do we care?

We collect a sample of [$n = 20$]{.alert} measurements, here it is:

```
35.16, 23.81, 32.65, 22.94, 32.35,
33.57, 37.94, 33.08, 22.13, 32.05,
25.24, 36.67, 28.64, 33.49, 27.11,
27.55, 26.89, 37.60, 34.26, 27.82
```

The mean is `30.548` cm

But the *historic* mean length of uhu was 42 cm.  So do our data give us confidence they are really smaller today?

# Confidence Intervals

## 4. Calculate [confidence intervals]{.alert} using the [standard error of the mean]{.alert}

Note: We can calculate CIs for any parameter, but for now we'll focus on the CIs of the mean

## 4. Calculate [confidence intervals]{.alert} using the [standard error of the mean]{.alert}

Recall that the mean $\pm$ 2 standard deviations covers roughly 95% of the probability of different values

```{r, fig.width=3, fig.height=2.5, fig.align='center'}
par(mar = c(2, 1, 2, 0) + 0.5)
denFill(rnorm(10000000), main = "mean = 0, sd = 1", xlim = c(-4, 4), yaxt = "n")
mtext("Probability density", 2)
text(0, 0.1, "95% of\nprobability")
```

## 4. Calculate [confidence intervals]{.alert} using the [standard error of the mean]{.alert}

The [confidence interval]{.alert} is a range of values surrounding the sample estimate that is
likely to contain the true population parameter

It is simply the mean $\pm$ 2 [standard errors]{.alert}

## Are uhu smaller now than in the past?

```{r, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
x <- c(35.16, 23.81, 32.65, 22.94, 32.35,
       33.57, 37.94, 33.08, 22.13, 32.05,
       25.24, 36.67, 28.64, 33.49, 27.11,
       27.55, 26.89, 37.60, 34.26, 27.82)

se_x <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
lower_ci <- mean(x) - 2 * se_x
upper_ci <- mean(x) + 2 * se_x

colz <- viridis::viridis(3)[2]

ggplot() +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci, y = 1),
                   height = 0.1, color = colz) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mean(x), y = 1), size = 3, color = colz) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 42, size = 1, color = colz) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    labs(x = "Uhu, mean length (cm)", y = "") +
    xlim(lower_ci - 10, 42 + 10) +
    ylim(0.5, 1.5) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
          axis.line.y = element_blank()) +
    annotate("text", x = mean(x), y = 1.05, label = "present mean and 95% CI",
             hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.5) +
    annotate("text", x = 42, y = 1.05, label = "historic mean",
             hjust = -0.1, vjust = -0.5)
```

## Confidence interval of the mean

Imagine a single sample with mean $\bar{Y}$ collected from a population

The population has a true mean value $\mu$

The 95% confidence interval for the mean is $\bar{Y} \pm 2 \times \text{SE}$

95% of the time, the 95% confidence interval will overlap the true (but unknown) population mean

## Confidence interval of the mean

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="50%"}
df <- tibble(
  x = 0.1,
  y = 0,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 0,
  xmin = -0.9, xmax = 1.1
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax), height = 0,
                 show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", -0.9, 0, label = "lower\nlimit", vjust = -0.25, size = 18) +
  annotate("text", 1.1, 0, label = "upper\nlimit", vjust = -0.25, size = 18) +
  annotate("text", 0.1, 0, label = expression(italic(bar(Y))), vjust = -0.5, size = 18) +
  annotate("label", 0, 0.05, label = expression(mu), size = 18) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 1.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.1, 0.1)) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )
```

## Confidence interval of the mean

Sometimes the confidence interval will not include the population parameter

The confidence interval in red does not include $\mu$

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="50%"}
df <- tibble(
  x = c(0.1, 1.1),
  y = c(-0.5, 0.5),
  ymin = y, ymax = y,
  xmin = x - 1, xmax = x + 1,
  color = LETTERS[1:2]
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = color)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  geom_point(size = 10, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax), height = 0,
                 show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
  annotate("label", 0, 0.05, label = expression(mu), size = 18) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )
```

## 95% confidence intervals

On average, 19 of 20 CIs will include the population parameter

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="70%", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ci_rand <- function(nrep, size, bias = 0, seed = 123) {
    mu <- 0
    sig <- 1

    set.seed(seed)

    # draw ybar from sampling dist
    ybar <- rnorm(nrep, mu, sig / sqrt(size))

    # sd^2 * (n-1) is chisq distrib with df n - 1, so se is this...
    se <- sqrt(rchisq(nrep, size - 1) / (size - 1) / size)

    lwr <- ybar - 2 * se + bias
    upr <- ybar + 2 * se + bias

    res <- data.frame(ybar = ybar + bias,
                      se = se,
                      lwr = lwr,
                      upr = upr,
                      overlap = lwr <= mu & upr >= mu,
                      r = rank(ybar))

    return(res)
}

ci_show <- function(df) {
    ggplot(df, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                       show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
        scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
        geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
        theme_cowplot() +
        theme(
            axis.title = element_blank(),
            axis.text = element_blank(),
            axis.line.y = element_blank(),
            axis.ticks = element_blank()
        )
}

df <- ci_rand(nrep = 20, size = 10, seed = 868239)

ci_show(df)
```

## Different levels of confidence

95% Confidence Intervals ara a common choice, but we could choose any percent

::: {.pause-think}
Will 90% confidence intervals be wider or narrower than 95% confidence intervals?
:::

## 90% CIs are narrower than 95% CIs

18 of 20 CIs include the population parameter

Less stringent CIs are narrower because they do not have to include the population parameter as often

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="70%"}
df1 <- mutate(df, lwr = ybar - 1.8 * se, upr = ybar + 1.8 * se) |>
    mutate(overlap = (lwr <= 0 & upr >= 0))

ci_show(df1)
```

## Bias shifts the sampling distribution

* If your sample is biased, increasing sample size doesn't help
* Because of increased precision, you're estimate is probably farther from the population parameter

## Bias shifts the sampling distribution

Confidence intervals from biased samples will include the population parameter less often

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="60%"}
df$bias <- "Unbiased"
df2 <- ci_rand(20, 10, 0.75, 868239)
df2$bias <- "Biased"

df3 <- rbind(df, df2)

ggplot(df3, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
    facet_grid(cols = vars(bias)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                   show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
    geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )
```

## Pseudoreplication leads to overconfidence

Pseudoreplication occurs when two sampled units are not independent

* Multiple measurements from the same patient
* Genetic variation of related individuals
* Species within the same genus

Usually, this leads to overconfidence because we've underestimated the spread of the sampling distribution

Pseudoreplication can occur with or without bias

## Pseudoreplication leads to overconfidence

With pseudoreplication, our CIs are too narrow, meaning **overconfident**. That overconfidence leads to failing to include the population parameter more often

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="60%"}
df$random <- "All independent"
df4 <- mutate(df, lwr = ybar - 1 * se, upr = ybar + 1 * se) |>
    mutate(overlap = (lwr <= 0 & upr >= 0))
df4$random <- "Pseudoreplicated"

df4 <- rbind(df, df4)

ggplot(df4, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
    facet_grid(cols = vars(random)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                   show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
    geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )
```

## [Pause & Think]{.alert}

Compared to the 95% confidence interval of a sample of size $n = 10$, would the 95% confidence interval of a sample of size $n = 20$ be wider or narrower?

## [Error bars]{.alert}

- Standard error of the mean or CIs are most common
- Clearly label if error bars are $\pm$ 1 SE, 2 SE, $s$, etc.
- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show*

## [Error bars]{.alert}

- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show*

If the spread of the data, show standard deviation (or just use a box plot which shows inner quartile range)

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.5}
set.seed(123)
dat <- data.frame(group = rep(LETTERS[1:2], 20),
                  y = rnorm(40))
dat$y[dat$group == "B"] <- dat$y[dat$group == "B"] + 2

gd1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    ggtitle("Data with\nSD error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

gd2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    ggtitle("Boxplot")

plot_grid(gd1, gd2)
```

## [Error bars]{.alert}

- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show*

If the estimate of the mean and its uncertainty, show standard error or confidence intervals

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.5}
gm <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, color = "gray") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

gm1 <- gm +
    ggtitle("Mean with\nSE error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

gm2 <- gm +
    ggtitle("Mean with\n95% CI error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - 2 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + 2 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

plot_grid(gm1, gm2)
```
